The finetooth shark (Carcharhinus isodon) exhibits a relatively small body size compared to many carcharhinids, with females reaching an ultimate total length of 190 centimeters [Li = 190 centimeters]. This asymptotic size is attained after a protracted period of somatic growth following the pupping event. Newborn individuals emerge at a modest size, with the total length at birth measured at 58.5 centimeters [Lb = 58.5 centimeters], though litter surveys indicate a broader range from 51 to 64 centimeters (51-64 centimeters) [Lb = 51-64 centimeters]. The age at birth has been estimated to be approximately 305 days [ab = approximately 305 days] based on captive observations conducted at a water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This gestation period, spanning roughly ten months, is consistent with the matrotrophic reproductive strategy typical of the genus Carcharhinus and likely reflects the energetic demands of uterine embryo development. The timing of parturition appears to be linked to seasonal temperature cycles in the coastal waters of the western North Atlantic, where pupping grounds are established in late spring. Neonates quickly disperse into shallow nursery habitats that offer abundant prey resources and reduced predation pressure, facilitating the critical transition to independent foraging.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs at different body sizes between the sexes, a pattern observed in many elasmobranchs with sexual size dimorphism. Males attain puberty at a total length of 118.7 centimeters [Lp = 118.7 centimeters], whereas females become reproductively mature only after reaching a somewhat larger size, with the total length at puberty for females recorded at 123 centimeters [Lp = 123 centimeters]. This divergence suggests that females require a prolonged juvenile phase to accumulate sufficient energy reserves and somatic mass to support the costs of gestation. The sub-adult period is a critical life stage characterized by rapid growth and high feeding rates on small teleost fishes, particularly menhaden and anchovies. Puberty itself is marked by distinct reproductive activation, including testicular recrudescence in males and ovarian maturation in females, which typically occurs coincident with the onset of warmer spring waters. The acquisition of reproductive status is not strictly tied to age alone; rather, body condition and prey availability interact to determine the timing of this developmental milestone across the species' range.

Reproductive output in the finetooth shark is moderate relative to its body size and aligns with a K-selected life history strategy. Gravid females produce between 1 and 6 pups per litter [N_R_i = between 1 and 6 pups per litter] and typically deliver a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], reflecting the maximum annual reproductive rate under favorable conditions at 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. The maximum daily reproductive rate corresponds to approximately 0.011 pups per day [Ri = approximately 0.011 pups per day] at the same thermal regime. This annual reproductive cycle is synchronized with seasonal shifts in water temperature, which influence both gestation duration and the timing of parturition in coastal nursery areas. The number of offspring per event is variable and appears to correlate positively with female body size, with larger females provisioning more pups per pregnancy. The reproductive frequency of one litter per annum is typical for sharks of this body plan and contrasts with the biennial cycles observed in some larger carcharhinids. Such reproductive constraints likely stem from the high energetic investment required for aplacental viviparous development, where embryos rely on yolk reserves supplemented by maternal histotroph. This modest fecundity emphasizes the importance of juvenile survival to population persistence.

The maximum lifespan of the finetooth shark has been inferred from back-calculated ages derived from vertebral growth bands, with the oldest documented individuals reaching approximately 14.4 years [am = approximately 14.4 years] in populations inhabiting waters maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This longevity is modest relative to many other members of the family Carcharhinidae, which may live several decades, and likely reflects the species' relatively small ultimate body size and faster metabolic pace. Life span completion occurs through natural mortality associated with senescence and age-related physiological deterioration, though fishing pressure also truncates survival in exploited populations. The ultimate wet weight attained by adult females is estimated at 55,500 grams [Wwi = 55,500 grams], a body mass that is closely correlated with the asymptotic length through a length-weight relationship developed from field-caught specimens. This maximum recorded body mass in adult females represents a substantial investment in both somatic and reproductive tissues. The interplay between growth trajectory, reproductive output, and longevity positions Carcharhinus isodon as a relatively fast-living member of its genus, with life-history traits that render it vulnerable to overfishing when mortality rates exceed recruitment capacity.

Coastal ecosystem associations of the finetooth shark are pronounced, with this species showing a strong preference for shallow, turbid waters along the southeastern United States. Juvenile sharks occupy low-salinity estuaries and river mouths that provide refuge from larger predators, while mature individuals undertake seasonal migrations along the continental shelf in pursuit of prey aggregations. These movements are tightly coupled with thermal habitat use, as the species is intolerant of cold water and typically remains within the 20 to 30 °C isotherms. The diet of Carcharhinus isodon is dominated by small schooling fishes, with menhaden and anchovies comprising the bulk of stomach contents across all life stages. Given its moderate longevity of about 14.4 years [am = about 14.4 years], the species exhibits an annual natural mortality rate that is balanced by successful pupping events, with each reproductive female contributing a limited number of offspring annually at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. Population modeling suggests that recruitment is strongly dependent upon the availability of intact nursery habitats. Conservation concerns have been raised in recent decades owing to directed commercial fisheries and incidental capture in shrimp trawls, underscoring the need for habitat protection and size-limit regulations to safeguard the species' unique life history.
